summary: Presents a base YANG data model for connection-oriented Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) protocols, giving a technology-independent view of the key OAM ideas. Technology-specific models can extend it, which keeps management uniform across protocols and supports nested OAM workflows. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: When you check a phone line, you do the same kinds of tests whatever kind of line it is. This document writes down a common checklist form so tools can test many different kinds of network connections the same way.

subtitle: A common YANG management model for the ping-and-traceroute style tools of connection-oriented networks.

tldr.problem: Many connection-oriented technologies have their own, similar OAM tools for checking reachability and finding faults, and each is managed differently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC takes the Maintenance Domain, Association and End Point structure of IEEE 802.1Q Connectivity Fault Management and turns it into a technology-independent YANG data model with RPCs for continuity check, connectivity verification and traceroute.
tldr.outcome: Technology-specific models such as TRILL and MPLS-TP can extend the base model instead of redefining it, and users can run the same commands on any of them, including drilling down level by level.

today: RFC 8531 is a Proposed Standard from April 2019 and the text shows no obsoleting or updating RFC. It is the base model that technology-specific OAM YANG models, such as those for TRILL and MPLS-TP, are meant to extend.

sections.title: Why a Generic OAM Model
sections.content:
OAM (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) covers three jobs: monitoring communications (reachability verification and Continuity Check), troubleshooting failures (fault verification and localization) and monitoring service-level agreements and performance. Over the years, many technologies built similar tools for these jobs.

In a connection-oriented technology, a connection is set up before data flows, and no extra control information is needed to carry user data afterwards. Ethernet Connectivity Fault Management (CFM) in IEEE 802.1Q is a widely adopted OAM standard, and ITU-T G.8013, MEF Service OAM, MPLS-TP (RFC 6371) and TRILL (RFC 7455) all build on its manageability framework. RFC 8531 therefore takes the CFM model, makes it technology-independent and defines the matching YANG data model.

The model supports generic continuity check, connectivity verification and path discovery (traceroute). The companion model for connectionless OAM is in RFC 8532.
sections.eli5: Lots of network types have their own tools to ask 'is this path working?'. This document makes one shared way to control all of them, like one remote that works for many TVs.

sections.title: A Base Model That Others Extend
sections.content:
The generic model is the root for other OAM YANG models. Technology-specific models, such as TRILL OAM or MPLS-TP OAM, inherit constructs from it without redefining them. The RFC gives three reasons: each model stays smaller, models can be developed independently, and an implementation can support only the models that apply (a TRILL RBridge may need only the generic model and the TRILL model).

The model lives at the management layer. Encapsulations and state machines still differ per OAM protocol, but a user who wants a Continuity Check, a Loopback or a performance monitoring session issues it the same way regardless of protocol, technology or vendor.

That uniformity enables a nested OAM workflow: after a failure is seen end to end, the user can drill down to lower-level segments of the path and use Loopback Message (fault verification) and Linktrace Message (fault isolation) with the same API, without changing the underlying protocols.
sections.eli5: There is one main rulebook, and each network type adds its own small page of extra rules. If a long trip fails, you can check each smaller piece of the road using the same tools.

sections.title: Domains, Associations and End Points
sections.content:
The model has three levels. At the top is the Maintenance Domain (MD), which has a name and a domain level. The container domains holds a list of MDs keyed by technology and md-name-string. Name formats are extensible: md-name-format is an identityref and md-name is a choice/case construct that derivative work can augment.

Under each MD there are one or more Maintenance Associations (MAs), keyed by ma-name-string and extensible in the same way. In TRILL, an MA can correspond to a Fine-Grained Label.

Under each MA there can be two or more Maintenance End Points (MEPs), keyed by mep-name. A MEP can be identified with an integer (mep-id-int) and addressed by a MAC address or an IP address, and the model is built to accept other addressing schemes. The MA and MEP also carry settings such as cos-id and cc-enable.

The module also defines notifications, sent when a defect is detected and when it clears. They carry the MD name, MA name, defect type, generating MEP ID and a defect message. A grouping for monitoring statistics, such as CCM transmit, receive and error counts, is for technology-specific modules to use.
sections.eli5: Think of a school (the domain), a class inside it (the association) and the students in that class (the end points). Each level has a name, and you can look up any of them.

sections.title: The OAM Commands (RPCs)
sections.content:
Commands are YANG RPCs, kept separate from the domain hierarchy. They give uniform APIs for the main OAM actions. The base module defines three:

  • continuity-check: verifies that a destination is reachable, also called reachability verification.
  • continuity-verification: verifies that the destination is connected through the expected path, which allows detection of unexpected topology changes.
  • traceroute: discovers the path, with a response list that can include the Maintenance Intermediate Point (MIP) that answered.

Inputs include the domain, level and association, ttl, a source MEP, a destination MEP (by MAC address, IP address or MEP ID), a count and a packet size. Each command is guarded by a feature (for example continuity-check, connectivity-verification, traceroute).

The RFC also separates proactive OAM, carried out continuously and needing persistent configuration, from on-demand OAM, started manually for a limited time and needing only transient configuration.
sections.eli5: The model has three buttons: 'Can you hear me?', 'Are we connected the way we expect?' and 'Show me every stop on the way.' You press them the same way on any network.

sections.title: Base Mode for Zero-Touch Use
sections.content:
To give a zero-touch experience, the RFC defines a default Base Mode with default values for the model's parameters. The default configuration MUST be present in devices that comply with the document, and its data nodes are read-only. The actual defaults depend on the technology; for example, Base Mode for TRILL is defined in RFC 7455.

The generic defaults are:

  • The MEP address is by default the IP address of the interface where the MEP sits.
  • Each device creates a single MEP on a virtual OAM port with no physical layer, with MEP-ID 0. The MEP-ID is 2 octets by default, and the IP address cannot be used because it is a much larger field.
  • CCM MUST NOT be used in Base Mode and MUST be disabled on the Base Mode MA. If CCM is needed, users MUST configure a separate MA with unique MEP IDs.
  • The MD name is the string GenericBaseMode. The Short MA Name format is a 2-octet integer (value 3) and the name is 65532 (0xFFFC).

CFM defines MEP-ID as an unsigned integer from 1 to 8191. This RFC proposes extending the range to 0 to 65535, with 0 reserved for Base Mode.
sections.eli5: Brand-new devices come with settings already filled in, like a game that starts with default options. Nobody has to set anything up before the first test.

sections.title: Extending It for TRILL and MPLS-TP
sections.content:
Section 7 shows, with snippets only, how technology models plug in. The complete extensions are left to the respective working groups.

For TRILL, the TRILL OAM module defines a technology identity trill, augments the MA with a connectivity context (a 12-bit VLAN ID or a 24-bit Fine-Grained Label), adds a 2-octet RBridge nickname as a MEP address case, adds a flow-entropy field for ECMP path selection, and extends the continuity-check and path-discovery RPCs with TRILL-specific parameters.

For MPLS-TP, the module defines the identity mpls-tp and a technology-sub-type to tell encapsulations apart, such as IP/UDP and PW-ACH. MPLS-TP MEP-IDs are either variable-length label values (G-ACH encapsulation) or 2-octet unsigned integers (IP/UDP), and the base int32 choice covers them without change.
sections.eli5: The base kit is like a plain LEGO set. TRILL and MPLS-TP each add their own special pieces on top, but the plain pieces stay the same.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The module is designed to be accessed through NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040). The mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH for NETCONF and TLS for RESTCONF, and the Network Configuration Access Control Model (RFC 8341) can restrict users to a subset of operations and content.

The writable lists, namely the domain, MA, MEP and session lists, may be sensitive. Unauthorized writes can lead to inconsistent configuration, reporting and presentation of the OAM mechanisms used to manage the network.

IANA registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-connection-oriented-oam and the YANG module ietf-connection-oriented-oam with prefix co-oam.
sections.eli5: Only trusted people should be allowed to change these settings. Otherwise someone could mix up the checks and the reports about the network would be wrong.

items.label: Reachability
items.desc: Verifies that a destination is reachable.

items.label: Path verification
items.desc: Verifies the destination is reached through the expected path.

items.label: Path discovery
items.desc: Discovers the path, with a response list that can include MIPs.
